tips.title: Mass never really changes
tips.body: In every reaction the mass of the products **equals** the mass of the reactants. When a balance appears to disagree, a **gas** has entered or left an open container. Nothing has been created or destroyed — it has just walked in or out of the measurement.

tips.title: Gains oxygen, gains mass
tips.body: A metal burning in air **gains** mass, because oxygen atoms from the air join the solid. A carbonate decomposing **loses** mass, because carbon dioxide leaves. Ask which way the gas is travelling and the direction of the change follows.

tips.title: One mole weighs its Mr in grams
tips.body: One mole of any substance has a mass in grams **numerically equal to its relative formula mass**. One mole of water is 18 g, one mole of calcium carbonate is 100 g. That single sentence turns every mass into an amount.

tips.title: The triangle that is really a division
tips.body: **moles = mass ÷ Mr.** Rearranged: *mass = moles × Mr* and *Mr = mass ÷ moles*. If the mass is in grams the answer is in moles — and if a question gives you kilograms or tonnes, convert to grams first or every later step is wrong.

tips.title: Uncertainty is half the range
tips.body: Repeat a measurement, take the **mean**, then quote the **range** about it: for 25.2 cm³ with a range of 0.2 cm³, write **25.2 ± 0.1 cm³**. AQA asks for the range about the mean as the measure of uncertainty, not a standard deviation.

why.matters:
Mass is conserved in every reaction, and a balance in a school lab will still tell you otherwise. Both are true: the reading changes because a **gas** entered or left an open container, and the missing mass is somewhere in the room.

Getting that straight is the first half. The second is the **mole**, which exists because a reaction is a conversation between particles and a balance can only weigh grams. The mole is the exchange rate between the two.

examples.title: The ribbon that weighs more after it burns
examples.body:
Burn magnesium in an open crucible and the white ash left behind weighs **more** than the ribbon did — which looks like a violation of the first rule in chemistry, and is not.

Each magnesium atom, mass 24, picks up an oxygen atom, mass 16, from the air. The product is 40: the ribbon has gained **67%** of its own mass, and every gram of it came out of the air. Nothing was created. The balance was only ever weighing what was in the crucible.

props.caption: The gain came out of the air, which the balance never weighed

visual.alt: Three bars in proportion: twenty-four grams of magnesium taking sixteen grams of oxygen from the air to give forty grams of magnesium oxide, so the solid gains two thirds of its own mass

examples.title: A dozen for atoms
examples.body:
A reaction happens between **particles**, in whole-number ratios, and a balance can only weigh grams. The mole is the bridge: a fixed-size group of particles, chosen so that **one mole of anything weighs its relative formula mass in grams**.

That is the whole trick. Eighteen grams of water is one mole; a hundred grams of calcium carbonate is one mole. Weigh those out and you have equal numbers of particles, without ever counting one.

visual.alt: A table of three substances with their relative formula masses and the mass of one mole of each: water at eighteen grams, carbon dioxide at forty-four and calcium carbonate at a hundred

examples.title: Why a result is written with a ± after it
examples.body:
No measurement is exact. A balance reading to 0.01 g is not telling you the mass to better than half of that, and a burette read to the nearest 0.05 cm³ is not either.

So a careful result carries its **uncertainty**: half the smallest division, or half the range of repeated readings. It is not an admission of sloppiness — it is the difference between claiming 25.2 cm³ and claiming to know the third decimal place, and a question that asks you to evaluate a method is usually asking about exactly this.

visual.alt: A table of three instruments with the smallest division each can be read to and the uncertainty that follows, which is half of it: a balance, a burette and a thermometer

steps.title: When the balance seems to disagree
steps.body:
You already know that **no atoms are lost or made in a reaction**, so the mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants. Yet in the lab a balance often reads differently before and after. Both things are true, and the explanation is always the same: **a gas has crossed the boundary of the container**.

In a **closed** system — a sealed flask — nothing can enter or leave, and the balance reading does not change at all.

In a **non-enclosed** system — an open crucible, a beaker on a balance — a gas can come in or go out, and only the substances still inside get weighed.

**Two cases appear again and again in the exam.**

**A metal heated in air gains mass.** Magnesium burns: $$2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}$$ Oxygen atoms from the air become part of the solid, so the solid left behind is **heavier** than the metal you started with.

**A metal carbonate heated in an open container loses mass.** Calcium carbonate decomposes: $$\mathrm{CaCO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}$$ The carbon dioxide **escapes into the atmosphere**, leaving the metal oxide as the only solid, so the solid is **lighter**.

In **particle** terms, nothing is destroyed in either case. The atoms are all still there; some of them are simply in the air rather than on the balance pan.

steps.title: Measurements and uncertainty
steps.body:
Every measurement carries some **uncertainty**. A burette read to the nearest $0.05\text{ cm}^3$, a balance reading to $0.01\text{ g}$ — neither gives the true value exactly, and repeating the measurement gives slightly different answers each time.

**What AQA asks for** is simple and specific: repeat the measurement, find the **mean**, and use the **range** of the results about that mean as the measure of uncertainty.

**The method.**

1. Take several repeats.
2. **Mean** = the sum divided by the number of results.
3. **Range** = largest result − smallest result.
4. **Uncertainty** = half the range, written as *mean ± half-range*.

For the five titres 25.1, 25.3, 25.2, 25.15, 25.25 cm³:

- mean $= 25.2\text{ cm}^3$
- range $= 25.3 - 25.1 = 0.2\text{ cm}^3$
- uncertainty $= \pm0.1\text{ cm}^3$, so the result is $25.2 \pm 0.1\text{ cm}^3$

**A wide range means a less certain result.** Two sets can share a mean and differ completely in how much you should trust it, and the range is what tells you.

**An anomalous result** — one far from the others — is normally excluded **before** the mean is taken, and you should say that you have excluded it and why.

steps.title: The mole
steps.body:
*(Higher tier only.)*

Atoms are far too small to count, so chemists count them in a fixed-size group called the **mole**.

**One mole of a substance contains the same number of particles as one mole of any other substance.** That number is the **Avogadro constant**, $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ per mole. One mole of carbon atoms and one mole of carbon dioxide molecules contain the same number of particles — atoms in the first case, molecules in the second.

**The mass of one mole, in grams, is numerically equal to the relative formula mass.**

- one mole of water ($M_r = 18$) has a mass of $18\text{ g}$
- one mole of calcium carbonate ($M_r = 100$) has a mass of $100\text{ g}$

That gives the equation the whole of quantitative chemistry rests on:

$$\text{moles} = \frac{\text{mass in grams}}{M_r}$$

Rearranged, $\text{mass} = \text{moles} \times M_r$ and $M_r = \text{mass} \div \text{moles}$.

**Units matter.** The mass must be in **grams**. A question quoting kilograms or tonnes needs converting first — $1\text{ kg} = 1000\text{ g}$, $1\text{ tonne} = 1\,000\,000\text{ g}$ — and forgetting is the most expensive single slip in this topic.

**Moles apply to anything countable**: atoms, molecules, ions, electrons, even the formula units written in an equation.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
**Part A.**

1. A sealed flask contains reacting chemicals. What happens to the balance reading, and why?
2. Iron wool is heated in air in an open dish. Does the mass rise or fall? Explain in one sentence.
3. Write the equation linking moles, mass and $M_r$.

**Part B.**

4. Heating 10 g of calcium carbonate leaves 5.6 g of calcium oxide. What mass of gas escaped?
5. Five readings are 12.2, 12.4, 12.3, 12.3 and 12.8 g. Identify the anomaly, then find the mean and the uncertainty of the rest.
6. Calculate the number of moles in 4.4 g of carbon dioxide.

**Part C.**

7. A student says burning magnesium "breaks conservation of mass". Write a reply that corrects them using the particle model.
8. Calculate the mass of 0.05 moles of calcium carbonate, then the number of formula units it contains.
9. A reaction in an open beaker loses 0.44 g. The gas given off is carbon dioxide. How many moles of carbon dioxide were produced, and how do you know the mass was not destroyed?

For question 5, exclude the anomaly **before** taking the mean, and say so.

steps.title: Going deeper
steps.body:
**Say where the mass went, not just that it changed.** "The mass decreased because a gas escaped" earns more than "the mass decreased". Name the gas, and say the container was open.

**Use the particle model when asked to explain.** Atoms are **rearranged**, not created or destroyed; the atoms that appear to have vanished are in the air. A mark scheme asking you to "explain in terms of particles" wants exactly that sentence.

**Check your arithmetic against the equation.** If $25\text{ g}$ of $\mathrm{CaCO_3}$ gives $14\text{ g}$ of $\mathrm{CaO}$, then $11\text{ g}$ of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ must have left — and $56 + 44 = 100$ confirms it. A number that fails this check is wrong.

**Convert units before anything else.** Grams for moles, every time. A question in tonnes that is not converted produces an answer a million times too small, and every later step inherits the error.

**Quote uncertainty as the range about the mean.** $25.2 \pm 0.1\text{ cm}^3$, not a percentage and not a standard deviation.

**Exclude anomalies deliberately and say so.** "Excluding the 25.80 result, which is far from the others, the mean is…" earns the mark that silently dropping it does not.

**Remember what a mole counts.** One mole of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ **molecules** — but $3 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23}$ **atoms**, because each molecule holds three. Questions that ask for atoms rather than molecules are testing precisely this.

**A closed system is the control.** If a question offers a sealed flask, the balance reading does not change — and that is the evidence that mass is conserved in the open case too.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- **Mass is always conserved**: products weigh the same as reactants.
- A balance appears to disagree only when a **gas** enters or leaves an **open** container.
- **Metal + oxygen → mass rises**: oxygen atoms join the solid.
- **Metal carbonate → mass falls**: carbon dioxide escapes.
- In a **sealed** container the reading does not change.
- Explanations should use the **particle model**: atoms rearranged, not destroyed.
- **Uncertainty**: take repeats, find the **mean**, and quote **half the range** — $25.2 \pm 0.1\text{ cm}^3$.
- Exclude an **anomaly** before averaging, and say that you did.
- *(HT)* One mole contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ particles — the **Avogadro constant**.
- *(HT)* The mass of one mole in grams equals the **relative formula mass**.
- *(HT)* $\text{moles} = \dfrac{\text{mass in g}}{M_r}$, and $\text{mass} = \text{moles} \times M_r$.
- Convert kilograms and tonnes to **grams** first.
- One mole of $\mathrm{CO_2}$ is $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ molecules but three times as many atoms.

questions.prompt: What does the law of conservation of mass state?
options: Mass is always lost as gas during a reaction
The mass of a solid never changes in a reaction
Mass increases whenever a gas is produced
The mass of the products equals the mass of the reactants

questions.prompt: A sealed flask of reactants has a mass of 82.5 g. After the reaction is complete, what is the mass of the flask and its contents, in grams?
questions.solution: Nothing can enter or leave a sealed flask, so the mass is unchanged: **82.5 g**.

It increases

questions.solution: Copper combines with oxygen from the air to form copper oxide, and the oxygen atoms add to the mass of the solid.

questions.prompt: Heating 20 g of calcium carbonate leaves 11.2 g of calcium oxide. What mass of carbon dioxide escaped, in grams?
questions.solution: $20 - 11.2 = $ **8.8 g** of carbon dioxide. The mass has not been lost: it left as a gas.

For the readings 18.4, 18.6 and 18.5 cm³, what is the uncertainty in cm³, taken as half the range?
questions.solution: Range $= 18.6 - 18.4 = 0.2$; half of that is **0.1 cm³**, so the result is $18.5 \pm 0.1\text{ cm}^3$.

What is the mass, in grams, of 0.5 moles of calcium oxide? (Mr of CaO = 56)
A student heats a metal carbonate in an open crucible and the mass of the solid falls. Which explains why?
questions.solution: The carbonate decomposes into a metal oxide and **carbon dioxide**, for example $\mathrm{CaCO_3} \rightarrow \mathrm{CaO} + \mathrm{CO_2}$. The crucible is **open**, so the carbon dioxide escapes and is no longer weighed. No mass is destroyed — the atoms are now in the air.

questions.prompt: How many molecules are there in 0.2 moles of carbon dioxide? Give your answer in standard form to three significant figures, as a multiple of 10²³.
questions.solution: $0.2 \times 6.02 \times 10^{23} = 1.204 \times 10^{23}$, which is $\mathbf{1.20 \times 10^{23}}$ molecules to three significant figures.

questions.prompt: How many moles are there in 2 kg of calcium carbonate? (Mr = 100)
questions.solution: $2\text{ kg} = 2000\text{ g}$, so $\dfrac{2000}{100} = $ **20 mol**. Failing to convert to grams gives 0.02, a thousand times too small.

markScheme.description: converts 2 kg to 2000 g

questions.prompt: How many **atoms** are there in one mole of carbon dioxide, CO₂?
options: The Avogadro constant
Three times the Avogadro constant
Twice the Avogadro constant
Half the Avogadro constant
questions.solution: One mole contains $6.02 \times 10^{23}$ **molecules**, and each molecule holds **three** atoms — one carbon and two oxygen — so there are three times the Avogadro constant in atoms.

markScheme.description: three times

questions.prompt: A student claims that burning magnesium in air disproves conservation of mass, because the solid gets heavier. Which explains, in terms of particles, why they are wrong?
questions.solution: Magnesium reacts with **oxygen from the air**: $2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}$. The atoms are **rearranged, not created** — the oxygen atoms were already there, in the air, where the balance could not weigh them — so the **total** mass is unchanged. Density describes how tightly mass is packed, not how much there is, so it cannot explain a gain in mass.

markScheme.description: oxygen from the air joins the solid; atoms rearranged, total mass unchanged

options: Magnesium oxide is denser than magnesium, so the same atoms now weigh more
The gain is only a balance error, because hot solids always weigh more
Oxygen atoms from the air join the solid; atoms are rearranged, not made
Each magnesium atom gets heavier when it is heated, but no new atoms appear

questions.prompt: A reaction in an open beaker loses 0.88 g, all of it carbon dioxide. How many moles of carbon dioxide were produced? (Mr of CO₂ = 44)
questions.solution: The mass lost is the mass of gas: $\dfrac{0.88}{44} = $ **0.02 mol**.

markScheme.description: uses the mass lost as the mass of gas

questions.prompt: Two students each take five titres. Both have a mean of 24.50 cm³, but student A has a range of 0.10 cm³ and student B a range of 0.80 cm³. What does this tell you?
options: B's result is more certain, because a larger range covers a wider spread
Both results are equally certain, because the means are identical
A's result must be more accurate, because the range is smaller
A's result is more certain, because the smaller range means less spread
questions.solution: The **range** measures the spread, so A has the smaller uncertainty — $\pm 0.05$ against $\pm 0.40\text{ cm}^3$. Note it says nothing about **accuracy**: both could be equally far from the true value.

markScheme.description: A, smaller range means less spread

questions.prompt:
A student burns 2.4 g of magnesium in an open crucible and weighs the solid before and after. They find the mass has risen to 4.0 g. A second student heats 2.4 g of magnesium carbonate in an open crucible and finds the mass falls.

Explain both observations, and describe how the first student could use repeats to give an uncertainty for their final mass. (6 marks)
questions.solution:
The magnesium **gains** mass because it reacts with **oxygen from the air**: $2\mathrm{Mg} + \mathrm{O_2} \rightarrow 2\mathrm{MgO}$, and those oxygen atoms are now part of the solid on the balance. The rise of $1.6\text{ g}$ is the mass of oxygen that reacted.

The carbonate **loses** mass because it decomposes to the oxide and **carbon dioxide**, and the crucible is **open**, so the gas escapes into the atmosphere and is no longer weighed.

In both cases mass is **conserved**: atoms are rearranged, not created or destroyed. The apparent change is only a change in what is inside the container.

For the uncertainty, the student should **repeat** the experiment several times, calculate the **mean** final mass, and quote the **range about the mean** — half the difference between the largest and smallest results — as the uncertainty, excluding any anomalous result and saying that they have done so.

examTechnique.body:
When a mass appears to change, say **which gas** moved and **which way**, and that the container was **open**. A metal gaining oxygen gets heavier; a carbonate losing carbon dioxide gets lighter; a sealed flask does not change.

For moles, convert the mass to **grams** first, then divide by $M_r$. For uncertainty, take the **mean** of your repeats and quote **half the range** about it, excluding anomalies and saying so.
examinerErrors: Saying mass was "lost" rather than that a gas escaped.
Not naming the gas in an explanation.
Forgetting that the container must be open for the reading to change.
Dividing kilograms or tonnes by Mr without converting to grams.
Quoting uncertainty as a percentage instead of the range about the mean.
Dropping an anomalous result without saying so.
Treating one mole of CO2 as 6.02 x 10^23 atoms rather than molecules.
Confusing a small spread (precision) with closeness to the true value (accuracy).
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A grade 9 answer explains a mass change by naming the gas, its direction of travel and the open container, and backs it with the particle model — atoms rearranged, never destroyed. It checks its arithmetic against the relative formula masses in the equation, converts every mass to grams before touching the mole equation, and quotes uncertainty as the mean plus or minus half the range, with any anomaly excluded and named. It knows a mole of a compound counts formula units, so the number of atoms is a multiple of the Avogadro constant, and it distinguishes a small spread from a correct result.
